title: Kafka at the West Bank checkpoint: de-normalizing the Palestinian encounter before the law
thesis: Alternative filmic representations of the West Bank checkpoint de-normalize the encounter, revealing it as a manifestation of Agamben's state of exception and sovereign law.
theme_1_justification: Not addressed. The paper does not discuss information goods, dual-use, or technology transfer.
theme_2_justification: Tangential mention. The paper discusses the opacity and arbitrary authority of the checkpoint's 'law', but not in terms of algorithmic or data-driven epistemic authority.
theme_3_justification: Tangential mention. The paper discusses the checkpoint as a mechanism of continuous modulation of movement and securitization, but does not conceptualize the city as a programmable or algorithmic system.
theme_4_justification: Central argument. The paper focuses on the checkpoint as a mechanism of spatial destruction, 'spatio-cide', and home unmaking, drawing on Weizman and Hanafi.
key_quotes: the checkpoint has emerged as a quintessential trope within the contemporary Palestinian imagination, to such an extent that 'checkpoint narratives' have arguably come to assume a dangerously 'normalized' status as everyday, even iconic features of Palestinian existence.

the article argues that apprehension of the enduring oddity and abnormality of the checkpoint serves as a vital mode of critical resistance to the policies of 'spatio-cide' 'securitization' and colonialism exercised at the hands of the State of Israel through the checkpoint mechanism.

the checkpoint operates as a physical manifestation of the 'state of exception' exercised by Israel as 'sovereign law', according to which the Palestinian subject is reduced to the status of 'homo sacer'
policy_relevance: Suggests that de-normalization of checkpoint narratives is a form of resistance; references BDS movement in notes.
